rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all 10 compounds and identify the weakest separations. The retention window will guide gradient trimming, while 40 °C leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in both directions.

Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity at the lone unresolved pair. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving the time-score advantage while we check for new close pairs.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a shorter gradient for a faster fully resolved method. Keeping temperature and endpoints fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness on the two marginally resolved pairs.

Restore injection 2’s successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute while shifting the starting composition upward to shorten retention. This should largely preserve the critical separations while testing whether the early peaks remain adequately retained and resolved.

Test whether a further temperature increase can restore full resolution with the faster 10-minute gradient. Comparing directly with injection 3 will isolate temperature-driven selectivity changes; injection 2 remains the maximum-CRF benchmark.

Use a shallower gradient than injection 4 to improve its sole failing pair, while retaining 55 °C to protect the other critical separation. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, offering another candidate for maximum CRF with a narrower solvent window.

With maximum CRF already achieved, explore a cooler selectivity regime using a faster gradient to seek a shorter fully resolved method. Lower temperature may separate the central cluster in a different elution order, while the steeper gradient limits the retention-time increase.

Return to the successful 55 °C regime and test a shallower gradient with a higher starting organic fraction. This may increase the resolution margin of both critical pairs while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; monitor early-peak retention as well.

Slightly flatten injection 6’s successful gradient to increase the resolution margin of its weakest pair. Keeping its starting composition and temperature should preserve the other critical separation, with the last peak still expected before 10 minutes.

Test a faster, higher-organic method at 60 °C to see whether the previously coeluting pair separates after an elution-order reversal. Maximum CRF is already secured; this exploratory run seeks a shorter fully resolved alternative while checking for early-peak compression.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction strengthens the reversed-order separation seen in injection 10, while a shallower gradient protects neighboring pairs. Monitor the first two peaks closely because their retention and resolution may become limiting.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 °C to recover the central separation while retaining temperature’s benefit for the other critical pair. The low starting organic fraction protects early-peak resolution; the last peak is expected near the 10-minute scoring boundary.

Slightly flatten injection 8’s gradient from 0.050 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift its lone failing pair above R = 1.5. Its other critical pair had more margin, and the last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 13’s successful gradient to shorten the run while retaining some of its improved resolution margin. Both critical pairs should remain above 1.5, testing a faster alternative to the most comfortably resolved maximum-CRF method.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 while keeping its successful starting composition and temperature. This should preserve maximum CRF and clarify whether the nearly slope-insensitive critical pair retains adequate resolution margin.

Preserve injection 2’s successful starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the gradient earlier. Its last peak eluted at approximately 0.57 organic fraction, so a 0.65 endpoint should retain the maximum-CRF separation with a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic content.

Shorten injection 10’s gradient to test whether increased steepness improves its reversed-order critical pair enough to reach full resolution. This seeks a substantially faster maximum-CRF method, although the neighboring pair may become limiting.

Test the cooler side of injection 3’s selectivity window: lowering temperature should improve its failing central pair, but may weaken the other critical pair. This directly checks whether a faster fully resolved method exists at 50 °C while retaining the established maximum-CRF methods.

Test a slope of 0.046875 organic fraction per minute, between injection 14’s fully resolved condition and injection 8’s slightly under-resolved condition. This should shorten retention relative to injection 14 while preserving maximum CRF and a modest resolution margin.

Slightly steepen injection 6’s gradient to test the fastest fully resolved boundary at this starting composition. Its weakest pair may approach R = 1.5, but the last peak should move earlier, potentially matching injection 2’s speed with better resolution of the other critical pair.

Use a slope of 0.0625 organic fraction per minute, between successful injections 6 and 9, to balance the two critical resolutions. The trimmed endpoint should keep all peaks within the gradient and deliver maximum CRF with the last peak near 8 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 13’s gradient to approximately balance its two critical resolutions near R = 1.7. This tests a larger minimum-resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and preserving maximum CRF.

Preserve the starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope of the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method, injection 2, with a lower endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient ends, the separation should remain unchanged.

Preserve the successful gradient slope through the critical cluster, then hold at 0.50 organic fraction to test a lower-solvent method. The final compound will elute during the hold; this run checks whether it still arrives before 10 minutes without sacrificing full resolution.

Test a slightly shallower variant of injection 22 to check the resolution margin around its balanced critical pairs while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already achieved; injection 16 remains a demonstrated faster option with a trimmed gradient endpoint.
